definition: Treating serious matters with careless, offhand disregard.
example: Her cavalier attitude toward deadlines frustrated the rest of the team.
nuance: Nonchalant just means calmly unconcerned, while cavalier suggests careless disrespect toward something that deserves attention.
prompt: A homeowner learns that the roof might leak during tomorrow's storm.
options: His cavalier shrug at the warning left the roofer shaking her head.
The cavalier homeowner hired two roofers and inspected every shingle herself.
Feeling cavalier, he politely held the door for the roofer and offered her lemonade.
The leak was so cavalier that water dripped steadily onto the couch.
reasons: Shrugging off a real risk to the house shows offhand disregard for a serious problem.
Careful, thorough action is the opposite of brushing off a danger.
This confuses the word with chivalrous; good manners are not careless disregard.
The word describes a person's attitude, so a leak cannot be cavalier.

practice.prompt: A student borrows a friend's expensive camera for a weekend trip.
options: Being cavalier, he wrapped the lens in soft cloth and returned the camera early.
Cavalier with cameras, he adjusted every setting as smoothly as a professional.
The cavalier camera captured sharp photos even in the dim evening light.
She was cavalier with the camera, tossing it into her bag without its case.
reasons: Protecting the camera and returning it early shows care, not disregard.
The word is about careless indifference, not skill or expertise.
A device has no attitude, so it cannot treat anything with disregard.
Handling someone else's valuable gear so carelessly shows a dismissive attitude.
